Scampering claws dig deep into the tree bark as the large lizard climbs higher, searching for a better vantage point. Within moments, 
a feathered blur passes the canopy clearing, and with instinctual precision, the ynill lets loose a stream of dark venom, blinding the 
hapless bird and dropping it down onto the trees below. Quickly,  the ynill rushes across the branches to claim it before it falls to the 
floor below. Th ese ranged predators hunt alone once mature, spending most of their day basking in the sun above the canopy. When 
courting for prospective mates, the males can be found gripping the fragile branches of the tallest trees, spitting their stream of venom 
as high into the sky as possible, in an effort to impress the darker green females watching from behind the leaf cover.

Encountering Preferring the heights of the canopy, ynnil often 
have their sights set above for flying creatures more than what 
walks along the ground. Felling the tree they can be found in is 
one sure way to get them closer, if excessive. Another is climbing 
up after them at night as they tend to be more passive and slow 
when the heat of the day cools down.
Strong digits with fortified claws 
allow the lizard to effortlessly climb 
trees. Scaling to the upper branches 
to better snipe their feathered prey
The forest canopy above can spell danger 
from aerial predators, and a crest of thorny 
scales along the ynnil’s neck and shoulders 
protect it from both talons and tooth
A thin hole in the lower mandible compresses venom 
glands that run beneath the lizard's tongue to allow 
a long stream of spraying venom. The caustic venom 
burns to the touch when exposed to air, and can 
effectively blind a creature for hours
